after: ## Relationships and the words that signal them
alt: Ten families of transitions, each with a symbol, examples and what the reader expects next: addition, contrast, concession, cause or result, example, sequence, emphasis, similarity, summary and qualification.
caption: Choose the relationship first, then the word that names it.

after: ## Matching the transition to the logic
alt: The same first fact, the council cut bus fares, followed by “As a result, ridership rose” and “However, ridership fell”: the transition tells the reader how to take the second idea. Below, “The shop sells fruit. Therefore, it is on Park Road” is wrong because no result exists.
caption: A transition only reveals logic that is already there; a false one misleads.

after: ## Transitions that introduce and relate evidence
alt: Six evidence-framing transitions with what each signals: “For instance” an example, “According to a recent survey” a source to weigh, “A second case supports this” more of the same, “In contrast” complicating evidence, “More telling still” stronger evidence, and “Even so” evidence that survives a challenge.
caption: Evidence transitions help the reader weigh and connect each piece.

alt: Three larger transitions, each in the centre with arrows back and forward: “Cost is only half the story” links money to the next topic; a short paragraph turns from what the shops gain to what the town loses; “Having seen what the lane costs, we must ask what it saves” links cost to savings.
caption: Restate the last idea and introduce the next: a reliable link between paragraphs.

after: ## Weak and strong versions side by side
alt: The weak skate-park paragraph is five unconnected sentences. The strong version labels each transition: “as a result” (cause), “In the year after it opened” and “which suggests” (framing evidence), “however” (contrast), “Even so” (concession) and “since” (reasoning).
caption: Name each relationship and the reader no longer has to guess.

after: ## Worked example 2: transitions in a published passage
alt: Lincoln’s sentences as a branching diagram: the shared position “Both parties deprecated war” splits at “but” into two matching “rather than” clauses, one making war and one accepting war, which converge on the short sentence “And the war came.”
caption: “But” divides, “rather than” matches, and “And” makes the war feel inevitable.
